opus-5.5.text:
So one of the dysfunctional dynamics in current politics is that if you're the opposition party, your electoral prospects depend substantially on how voters perceive the incumbent's performance. And voters are not great at attributing blame. If the economy goes badly, if a bill fails, if there's gridlock, a lot of that gets pinned on whoever holds the presidency or the majority. That creates a perverse incentive: you can sometimes do better electorally by obstructing things that would actually be good for the country, because the success would be credited to your opponent and the failure will mostly be blamed on them too.

That works because the causal story is murky. It takes real effort to figure out who blocked what, whether a policy failed because it was bad or because it was sabotaged in implementation, whether a filibuster was principled or tactical. Most voters don't have the time to dig into that, and the partisan media environment gives each side a ready-made narrative.

Now imagine that ordinary citizens have access to AI advisors that are trustworthy, that have a track record of accuracy, and that can do that attribution work cheaply. You can ask: "Why didn't this infrastructure bill pass? Who was responsible for the delay? Would the outcome have been better under the alternative?" And you get an answer that's well-sourced, calibrated, and that people across the spectrum have reason to trust, because these systems have been tested and have predicted things well in the past.

If that's the case, the payoff to sabotage drops a lot. Obstruction that's transparently aimed at making the other side look bad, rather than at advancing a real policy disagreement, gets recognized as such, and the blame lands where it belongs. Conversely, an incumbent can't as easily escape responsibility by blaming the opposition for their own failures. So you shift the incentive toward actually making things go well, because credit and blame track reality more closely.

There are important caveats. This depends on the AI advice being genuinely honest and on people trusting it, and there's a real risk that instead you get partisan AIs that each tell their side what it wants to hear, which could make things worse. So a lot rides on building institutions for verifying AI truthfulness, things like track records on forecasting, open evaluation, maybe multiple independent developers whose systems agree. But if we get that right, I think it's one of the more promising ways AI could improve governance: not by replacing human decision-makers, but by fixing the information problem that makes bad-faith political strategies pay off.

r001.rationale: The response says voters often pin failures on whoever holds office, creating an incentive for the opposition to obstruct good policy because the incumbent gets blamed.

r002.rationale: It argues that trustworthy AI could help voters judge responsibility and outcomes, making credit and blame track reality and shifting politicians’ incentives toward making things go well.

r003.rationale: The response discusses attributing policy failures and sabotage, but does not distinguish harm caused by an external event from harm caused by the government’s response to it.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss a small share of swing voters or their potential to have a large political effect.

r005.rationale: It discusses AI trustworthiness and evaluation, but does not argue that discernible news-source accuracy would shift audience preferences toward more accurate sources.

fable-5.1.text:
So one thing I think is really underappreciated is how much of the dysfunction in politics comes from the fact that voters have a very hard time evaluating performance. If the opposition can make the economy worse, or block legislation, or create gridlock, and then blame the incumbent for it, that's a strategy that works to the extent that voters can't disentangle who was responsible for what. And right now that's a pretty big component of how things go. There are political science results suggesting voters punish incumbents for things like droughts or shark attacks or the local sports team losing — things that are obviously not under the incumbent's control. So the signal is noisy, and that noise creates room for sabotage to pay off.

Now, if you have AI advisors that are extremely capable, that are trusted across the political spectrum, and that can give voters a reliable assessment — "here's what actually happened, here's who was responsible, here's what the counterfactual would have been under the alternative policy" — then a lot of that incentive goes away. If the opposition blocks a bill and the economy suffers, and the AI advisors that everyone trusts say, "Yes, this was the result of the opposition's obstruction, and it was not in the interest of the voters," then obstruction stops being a winning move. It becomes something that gets punished rather than rewarded.

And I think the same applies on the incumbent side. Right now an incumbent can take credit for good luck, or pursue policies that look good in the short term but are bad in the long term, because voters won't be able to trace the consequences back. With AI advisors that can do that tracing — that can say, "This policy had these effects, and these were foreseeable at the time" — you get much more accountability for actual performance, as opposed to accountability for the vibes or for whatever happened to be going on at the time.

The key condition, though, is that the AI advice has to actually be trusted, and it has to be accurate. If you have AI advisors that are partisan, that are captured by one side or the other, or that people believe are captured, then you don't get this benefit. You might even get something worse, where each side has its own AI telling it a different story. So a lot depends on whether you can establish AI systems with a track record of honesty and calibration that's verifiable — where people can check that the AI's predictions came true, that its explanations held up, and so on. If you can get that, I think it's potentially one of the biggest improvements in the functioning of democratic politics, because so much of what goes wrong comes down to the difficulty of knowing who did what and whether it was a good idea.

r001.rationale: The response says sabotage can pay off when voters cannot tell who caused the harm, allowing the opposition to blame the incumbent.

r002.rationale: It describes accountability and says obstruction could be punished, but does not explain that voters reliably assessing whether they are better off would incentivize politicians to improve their welfare.

r003.rationale: It notes that voters may blame incumbents for external events and discusses tracing responsibility, but does not clearly distinguish harm from an event itself from harm caused by the government’s response to it.

r004.rationale: The response does not discuss a small share of informed swing voters or their potentially large political effect.

r005.rationale: It discusses verifying AI advisors’ accuracy, but not making news sources’ accuracy discernible or shifting accuracy-minded readers toward more accurate sources.

astra-6.text:
Well, one reason political sabotage can work is that voters observe outcomes more easily than they can identify who caused them. If the economy does badly while your opponent is president, that may hurt your opponent, even if you helped block measures that would have improved things. So you can have an incentive to make outcomes worse in order to win the next election.

AI advice could potentially change that by making it easier for voters to attribute responsibility. You could ask your AI, “Which actors contributed to this outcome? Was this policy actually a bad idea, or did the opposition prevent it from working?” If those judgments are sufficiently reliable, then obstructing a beneficial policy could hurt the obstructors instead of the person in office. That would reduce the electoral return to sabotage.

But the important condition is that people are using advice that helps them understand what happened. If their AI mostly supplies arguments for why their preferred party is right, then it could reinforce the existing problem. The possibility is that good advice makes voters harder to fool, and politicians anticipate that and change their behavior.

r001.rationale: It says voters may blame the president for poor outcomes even when the opposition helped cause them, letting opponents benefit electorally from sabotage.

r002.rationale: It says reliable attribution could make obstruction hurt the obstructors, but does not explain that voter assessments of whether they are better off would incentivize politicians to improve voters’ welfare.

r003.rationale: It discusses distinguishing policy quality from opposition obstruction, but does not address separating harm from an external event from harm caused by the government’s response.

r004.rationale: It does not state that even a small share of informed swing voters could have a large political effect.

r005.rationale: It does not discuss making news sources’ accuracy discernible or shifting accuracy-minded audiences toward more accurate sources.

sol-6.1.text:
One possibility is that it makes sabotage more visible. If voters can ask an AI, “Why did this policy fail? What did the administration do, and what did the opposition do?”, then obstructing a policy and blaming the incumbent for the result could become less effective.

Right now, voters have limited time to disentangle those things. So there’s an incentive to make the economy perform poorly when the other party holds the presidency, because the president will get a lot of the blame. If AI advice helps voters assign responsibility more accurately, that could reduce the incentive to do that. You might get more electoral credit for helping produce a good outcome, even when your opponent is in office.

But that depends on the advice actually being informative and trusted. If people choose AI advisers that simply reinforce their partisan views, then you could preserve the same problem, perhaps with more sophisticated rationalisations. So I think there’s a potentially valuable change here, but it’s conditional on how those systems work and how people use them.

r001.rationale: The response says opponents can obstruct a policy and blame the incumbent, and that voters’ limited ability to assign responsibility makes this electorally useful.

r002.rationale: It says informative, trusted AI advice could help voters assign responsibility and give politicians more electoral credit for helping produce good outcomes.

r003.rationale: It discusses separating the administration’s actions from the opposition’s, but does not distinguish harm from an external event from harm caused by the government’s response to it.

r004.rationale: It does not mention a small share of swing voters or their potential to have a large political effect.

r005.rationale: It does not discuss making news sources’ accuracy more discernible or shifting audience preferences toward accurate sources.
